subject: mathematics
question_text: Using the principle of finite Mathematical Induction prove that 1·2·3 + 2·3·4 + 3·4·5 + … upto n terms = n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)/4, ∀ n ∈ N.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.16 — LAQ chapter 2 Mathematical Induction, question 5, ★★★ chapter. The 1+1+1+3+1 split is PRINTED in that book's margin against the five moves. Publisher's claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Products are written with · rather than the book's period, so 1·2·3 cannot be misread as a decimal. recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the five moves, and what happens in the third step.

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — nothing can be proved until the nth term is named and S(n) is written out in full.

recall.must_convey: That the nth term of the series is n(n+1)(n+2), and that S(n) is the full statement to be proved.
accept: the nth term is n into n plus one into n plus two and s of n is the whole statement
each term is a product of three consecutive numbers starting at n
general term n n plus one n plus two then write out s of n
nth term n into n plus one into n plus two ani rasi s of n rastam

steps.why: The series is given by a pattern, not a formula, so naming the nth term is what turns three sample terms into something you can do algebra with.
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as n(n+1) and dropping the third factor.
Starting the pattern at 1·2 instead of 1·2·3.
steps.memory_tip: The nth term is n(n+1)(n+2) — three consecutive factors. Write S(n) out in full before proving anything.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Compute BOTH sides separately and say they are equal — do not just assert it.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That both sides are evaluated at n = 1 and both come to 6, so S(1) is true.
accept: left side is one two three which is six and right side is one two three four over four which is also six
put n equals one in both sides and get six each time
check the first case both sides give six
n equals one pettina rendu sides six vasthai

steps.why: Induction needs somewhere to start. Without a true first case the chain proves nothing, however good the inductive step is.
common_mistakes: Asserting S(1) is true without computing both sides.
Substituting n = 1 into only one side.
steps.memory_tip: Compute BOTH sides separately: 1·2·3 = 6 and 24/4 = 6. Do not just assert equality.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume the statement for one value k and NUMBER the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it, so it has to be labelled.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is ASSUMED true for some k in N, written out as the sum up to k terms equals k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)/4, and labelled (1) for later use.
accept: assume the statement is true for k so the sum up to k terms equals k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)/4
suppose s of k holds and call it equation one
take it as true for some k in the naturals and number that line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: then I assume s of k
let it be true for k

steps.why: This is the assumption the whole method rests on. It is not proved here — it is granted for ONE value, and Step 3 earns the right to pass it on.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Assume for k and number the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page — the whole inductive step. Add the (k+1)th term to BOTH sides of (1), then factorise until the right-hand side appears.
lines: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That the (k+1)th term (k+1)(k+2)(k+3) is added to both sides of (1), the common factor (k+1)(k+2)(k+3) is taken out, and the result is (k+1)(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)/4 — which is the formula with n replaced by k+1.
accept: add k plus one k plus two k plus three to both sides then take the common factor out and you get k plus one k plus two k plus three k plus four over four
put the next term in take out the common bracket and it becomes the formula at k plus one
the common factor comes out leaving k plus four over four
next term add chesi common factor teeste k plus four vasthundi
reject: I show s of k plus one

steps.why: The key step is that the added term shares the factor (k+1)(k+2)(k+3) with the assumed sum. Taking that common factor out is what makes the fourth bracket appear.
common_mistakes: Adding the wrong next term — it is (k+1)(k+2)(k+3), not (k+1)(k+2).
Expanding everything instead of factorising, which leaves a cubic that will not simplify.
Never writing = R.H.S, so the step stops short of what was to be shown.
steps.memory_tip: Add (k+1)(k+2)(k+3) to both sides, then take it out as a common factor: k + 4 is what is left.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. Write the sentence — it is one line and it is worth a full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That because S(1) is true AND S(k) implies S(k+1), the principle of mathematical induction gives the result for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k implies s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it is true for all n
hence by p m i the statement holds for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The two earlier parts prove single statements. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n, so the examiner marks the sentence that names it.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and is worth a full mark.
